Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Kwame was seventy-seven when he first sat in the intake chair, the folded PCL-5 form resting against his thigh, its total score of forty-four marking the threshold of his visit. He had crossed oceans and borders as a young man, part of a displaced crowd that moved through the night under the direction of armed patrols. He remembers the event not as a continuous story but as a series of frozen frames: a boot scuffing through dry earth, the harsh red glow of a flare against a corrugated roof, a heavy door clicking shut in a compound he would not see again. When he tries to speak of it now, he feels completely numb, as if he were reading a report about someone else's life. The emotional weight never traveled with the images. He holds onto those snapshots, each one isolated and still, and they sit quietly in the background of his days. The potency of certain moments in his life makes sense when viewed through that frame. The patrols had never negotiated, only directed, and the sudden expectation of immediate obedience had always preceded a violent shift in his circumstances. That is why the trigger of authority commands strikes him with such specific clarity today. Decades have passed, but certain moments still pull his attention. When a junior developer leans across his desk at the small consulting firm he runs from his Atlanta study and says, "Kwame, I need the architecture documentation finished by Friday," his breath catches. He was certain that the sharp tone, the expectation of immediate compliance, carried the same unyielding weight as the voices that once directed his movements. The room seems to tilt. What frightened him most was the quiet beginning of a feeling where the walls softened and his own hands looked unfamiliar. He was detached, floating just outside the furniture, watching a man in a chair try to breathe. He learned to step back, to let the words hang in the air while he counted the threads in his desk blotter until the sensation passed. These moments unfold in the same calendar as other routines that have settled into his life. He avoids going out when the sky is overcast or when television news broadcasts footage of displaced camps or military convoys, scenes that align too closely with his own snapshots. He avoids people in crowded elevators and long checkout lines, finding himself at home more often, filling his mornings and evenings with mental distraction. He reorganizes his legacy code repositories, runs background network diagnostics, keeps his mind occupied all the time. The consequences of these patterns are visible in the quiet corners of his life. His wife, Amara, notes the distance when she sets the table for one. They stopped planning trips to visit their grandchildren in Georgia. He missed his cousin's memorial service because the terminal security lines felt like a landscape he could not navigate without panic rising in his chest. His work continued, but he delegated client calls, working only from his study where he controlled the doors and the silence. At his current stage of life, Kwame sits at his kitchen table, looking at the clinical notes from his first session. He is not fractured, but he is tired of the architecture he has built. He came to seek help because his granddaughter asked why he rarely leaves the house anymore, and he realized he no longer knew how to answer. He is most afraid that the detachment will harden into something permanent, that he will spend his remaining years watching life through a pane of glass. He hopes, more than anything, to remember that he is safe now, to let his memories have weight again, and to walk into a room without bracing for the next command.
